en: On the Emperor’s Birthday, at the Linqide Hall,
the *Profound Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in one fascicle was expounded;
the śramaṇa Jingju of Daguang Temple respectfully presents this.
This sutra consists of seven locations and nine assemblies, comprising thirty-nine chapters and eighty fascicles in total.
The first is the Assembly at the Site of Enlightenment, which contains six chapters:
first, the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornments of the World-Ruler," in five fascicles;
1. Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata, one fascicle; 2.
Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra and Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World, these two chapters together comprise one fascicle;
3. Chapter on the Flower Treasury World, three fascicles.
The sixth is the "Vairocana Chapter," one fascicle.
This constitutes the second assembly, the Universal Radiance Hall Assembly, which comprises six chapters:
the seventh, "The Names and Titles of the Tathāgatas," and the eighth, "The Four Noble Truths"; these two chapters together form one fascicle.
The ninth chapter, "Awakening of Radiance," and the tenth chapter, "The Bodhisattva’s Inquiry on Clarification," together comprise one fascicle;
the eleventh chapter, "Pure Conduct," and the twelfth chapter, "Worthy Leader," together comprise two fascicles.
The third assembly, on the summit of Mount Sumeru, consists of six chapters:
Chapter Thirteen, "Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru"; Chapter Fourteen, "Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru"; and Chapter Fifteen, "The Ten Abodes.

These three chapters together comprise one fascicle; Chapter Sixteen, "Pure Conduct"; and Chapter Seventeen, "The Merit of First Resolving for Enlightenment. These two chapters together comprise one fascicle.
The *Eighteen Sections on the Clarification of Dharmas*, one fascicle.
The fourth assembly, the Night-Heaven (Yāma) Palace Assembly, consists of four sections:

Section Nineteen, "Ascending to the Night-Heaven Palace"; Section Twenty, "Verses of Praise within the Night-Heaven Palace"; and Section Twenty-one, "The Ten Practices. These three sections together comprise two fascicles.
The *Twenty-Twenty Inexhaustible Treasury Collection*, one fascicle.

The Fifth Assembly, the Tuṣita Heaven Palace Chapter, consisting of three sections: the twenty-third, "Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," one fascicle; [the twenty-fourth, "The Great Assembly of the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," one fascicle; and the twenty-fifth, "The Tuṣita Heaven Palace Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Former Deeds," one fascicle].
The twenty-fourth is the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Palace," and the twentieth is the "Chapter on the Fifty Dedications"; these two chapters together comprise eleven fascicles.
The sixth is the "Assembly in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations," which consists of one chapter:
the twentieth, the "Chapter on the Sixty Stages," comprising six fascicles.
The seventh assembly, the Hall of Universal Radiance, consists of eleven chapters:
Chapter 20, "The Seventy Samādhis," in four fascicles;
and Chapters 28, "The Eighty Pervasions," and 29, "The Ten Endurances," these two chapters together comprising one fascicle.
Chapter Thirty-one: The Lifespans of the Tathāgatas; Chapter Thirty-two: The Abodes of the Bodhisattvas—these three chapters together comprise one fascicle; Chapter Thirty-three:
The Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha, two fascicles; Chapter Thirty-four:
The Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata and Chapter Thirty-five: The Merits of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks—these two chapters together comprise one fascicle.
Chapter Thirty-Six: The Universal Practices of Samantabhadra, one fascicle;
Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Manifestation of the Tathāgata, three fascicles.
The eighth assembly, the Repeated Gathering in the Hall of Universal Radiance, consists of one chapter:
Chapter Thirty-eight: Leaving the World, seven fascicles.
Ninth Assembly: Jetavana, one chapter.
Chapter Thirty-nine: Entering the Dharma Realm, twenty-one fascicles.
Regarding the title *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka*: "Mahāvaipulya" (Great and Vast) refers to the Dharma;
"Buddhāvataṃsaka" (Flower Ornament of the Buddha) refers to the person.

Furthermore, "Great" (mahā) signifies the pervasiveness of the essence (*tattva*), while "Vast" (vaipulya) is named for the omnipresence of its function (*vṛtti*); thus, it is called "Great and Vast" because the function arises based upon the essence.
"Buddha" refers to the person who has realized and taught [the truth].
"Avataṃsaka" (Flower Ornament) signifies the adornment of the fruit through the cultivation of causes.
Since this sutra elucidates that meaning, it is called the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*.
This sutra consists of seven locations and nine assemblies, comprising thirty-nine chapters and eighty fascicles in total.
The first assembly takes place at the Aranya-dharma in the Bodhimaṇḍa.
The sutra consists of six chapters that clarify the virtues of the Buddha’s fruition.

When Vairocana first attained perfect enlightenment, the lords of the assemblies from the ten directions—including the Great Lord Maheśvara King and various bodhisattvas—along with forty such classes of similar retinues, each numbering as many as the atoms in a buddha-field, all arrived at the assembly; hence there is the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of Worldly Lords."
Once the ocean-like assembly has gathered and the Buddha manifests his true countenance, there is the "Chapter on the Marks of the Tathāgata.

Since the true marks are free from all marks and cannot be perceived by bodhisattvas of lesser capacity, the Great Being Samantabhadra enters the samādhi of mastery and realizes the realm of the Buddha; thus, there is the "Chapter on the Samādhi of Samantabhadra."

The Buddha possesses dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*); within this dependent retribution, first distinguishing the causal conditions that constitute it, there is the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World.
Next, clarifying the ocean of lands upon which he relies, there is the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World."

Since the environment and its rewards have been manifested, the magnificent and sublime ultimate fruition belongs to the Venerable One; therefore, there is the Vairocana Chapter. Furthermore, this first assembly serves as the realm for those who possess faith and joy.
The second assembly did not depart from the site of enlightenment; having accepted the invitation of the Dragon Palace, it is titled the "Assembly of the Universal Radiance Hall.
This scripture consists of six chapters, which elucidate the minds of those who possess faith.
The Buddha responds to sentient beings by first manifesting his three karmas:
when established according to his bodily karma, there is the "Chapter on the Names and Titles of the Tathāgata";
when expounding the teachings according to his verbal karma, there is the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths."
To alert the assembly by means of mental action, there is the "Chapter on Radiant Awakening.
Since the arising of right faith must first be preceded by right understanding, there is the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry for Clarification."
To understand without practicing is like seeking satiety by merely talking about food.
Because one establishes practice through understanding and understands through practice, there is the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (Śīlaparivarta).
Because practice serves as the cause for accomplishing virtue, which is the source of all wholesome qualities, there is the "Chapter on the Wise Head" (Bhadramukhaparivarta).
Although this second assembly clarifies right faith, it has not yet established the faculty of wisdom; thus, it is like light feathers that follow the wind without stability.
The third assembly does not depart from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), where the Buddha accepts the invitation of the Heavenly King and ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven palace.
The sutra consists of six chapters that give rise to the faculty of right wisdom.
Ascending to the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Master of Transformation attends the assembly.
In the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Trāyastriṃśa Palace," the assembly assists in the transformation by praising his virtues.
These two chapters should be understood as being based on the permanent.
The "Ten Abodes Chapter" distinguishes the understanding within the abodes;
the "Brahmacarya Chapter" clarifies the practice within the abodes.
The "Chapter on the Merit of Generating the Bodhicitta" elucidates the virtues of abiding [in the stages].
These three chapters correspond to the "Correct Teaching" (bhūmi).
The "Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma" corresponds to the "Progression" (pratipatti).
In this assembly, right wisdom has already become clear.
The fourth is the assembly where, without arising from the Bodhimanda, one ascends to the Suyama Heaven palace.
This sutra consists of four chapters; relying upon that faculty of wisdom, it gives rise to correct practice.
The Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven corresponds to the objects of the world through its perfect harmony;
the Chapter on Verses of Praise within the Yāma Palace possesses every virtue without exception.
These two chapters shall arise in that assembly.
The "Chapter on the Ten Practices" (Daśabhūmika) correctly elucidates the accomplishment of practice.
The "Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Stores" (Akṣayamatinirdeśa) subsumes the progress of practice.
Although this subsequent assembly establishes the roots and trunk, its branches and leaves have not yet been fully spread.
Fifth is the "Not Arising from the Site of Enlightenment" chapter, which describes ascending to the assembly in the Tuṣita Heaven palace.
This section consists of three chapters that clarify the dedication of merit and vows, universally shading all beings throughout the realms of sentient beings without exception.
The "Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace" clarifies that when the Buddha is moved by a response, there is nothing that does not manifest.
The "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Palace" signifies that among the assembly, there is no virtue that is not extolled.
The "Chapter on the Ten Dedications" (Daśapariṇāmanā-parivarta) constitutes the formal exposition of this assembly.
As for the term "dedication" (pariṇāmanā), it means dedicating oneself toward others, dedicating the small toward the great, and dedicating phenomena toward principle.
Through these three dedications, one realizes those three bodies.
The preceding five assemblies correspond to the stage of the three levels of the *śaikṣa* (the three stages of the noble ones).
The sixth assembly, the Immovable Bodhimanda, corresponds to the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
There is one chapter in the sutra that ascends to the ten sages (*ārya*), elucidating the abiding in the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, "worthy" (*xian*) means "good," while "sage" (*sheng*) means "correct.

As for what is called the "three," the ten abodes (*vihāra*) constitute the lower stage of worthiness; they are designated by name based on their application of wisdom (*prajñā*) and their severance of afflictions.
The ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are termed "Virtuous" (*satpuruṣa*), based on the cultivation and advancement of wholesome qualities;
the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are termed "Superior Virtuous" (*adhisatpuruṣa*), based on the supreme vows for the benefit of both oneself and others.
Thus, there are three types of sages.

However, the earth possesses the significance of generation and growth; it symbolizes that this untainted noble wisdom can produce the meritorious virtues of a Bodhisattva’s attainment of Buddhahood, and is therefore like the earth.
Turning one's back on the mundane and ascending to the sacred, severing hindrances and realizing the truth, one is newly born into the Buddha-family; therefore, it is named "Joyful" (Prāmodya).

Second is the Stage of Freedom from Defilement (Vimalā): by purely cultivating the three karmas, like gold refined by fire, one becomes free from the defilement of transgressing the precepts; therefore, it is named "Freedom from Defilement."

The third is the Ground of Radiant Emission (*Prabhākarī*): because one cultivates and realizes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), is able to manifest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and emits the light of wondrous wisdom, it is named "Radiant Emission.

The fourth is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*): because concentration can give rise to wisdom, and by means of the fire of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) consisting of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one burns the fuel of afflictions (*kleśa*), it is named "Blazing Wisdom."

The fifth is the Ground of Difficult Victory (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*): because the two types of knowledge—the ultimate and the conventional—have mutually opposing modes of activity, yet are joined so as to become harmonious, it is named "Difficult Victory.

The sixth is the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*): because the correct wisdom of *prajñā* realizes the twelve links of dependent origination, uproots the root of ignorance, enters the three gates of liberation, and the true principle of the emptiness of phenomena clearly manifests before one, it is named "Manifestation."

Regarding the seventh stage, the Ground of Far-Reaching Travel (*Dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*): it is characterized by constant abiding in samādhi, wherein the arising of functional activity remains unimpeded. Having transcended both existence and non-existence, it cannot be fathomed by those in lower stages.

While the preceding six stages were still accessible for common practice by humans, devas, and followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), this stage arises uniquely; therefore, it is called "Far-Reaching."

Regarding the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā): having realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one is no longer moved by the exertion of signs or conditioned activities.

Having received the seven exhortations from the Buddha, one gives rise to the ten bodies of marks and the ten masteries; within the swift current of the Dharma, one proceeds spontaneously without relying on deliberate mental effort, and is therefore called "Immovable."

Regarding the ninth stage, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*): whereas previously one realized the essence of the Dharma, now one gives rise to its function. One exclusively studies the sovereign conduct of the Dharma King regarding speech and silence, and manifests the characteristics of a sentient being endowed with the forty kinds of unimpeded eloquence. Acting as a great Dharma teacher, there is nothing one seeks that is not responded to; therefore, it is named "Excellent Intelligence."

Regarding the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*): the great cloud of dharma-wisdom can screen off defilements and delusions, and it is able to receive all the rain of the Buddhas' teachings; furthermore, it universally bestows this rain of dharma upon all classes of beings. Therefore, it is named the Cloud of Dharma.

Furthermore, the first, second, and third stages correspond to the conduct of humans and devas; the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages correspond to the conduct of the Two Vehicles; the seventh stage corresponds to the conduct of the Mahāyāna; and the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages enter the conduct of the One Vehicle; thus, there are ten types of sages.
The seventh is the Immovable Bodhimanda, the Hall of Universal Radiance where they gather once more; this scripture consists of eleven chapters.

The preceding sections clarified the stages and positions of the three grades of worthies and ten levels of sages as their practice was nearing completion; now, in this section, causes are perfected and fruits are fulfilled.
In the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," one cultivates thirteen samādhis and realizes that existence is non-existence.
In the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers," the ten wisdoms are illuminated, revealing that emptiness is non-emptiness.
In the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences," concentration and wisdom are balanced, and emptiness and existence are unified.
In the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*), since the numbers are so vast that calculation cannot reach them, it clarifies the breadth of his virtue.
The "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" exhausts the limits of the future in the vertical dimension;
the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas" pervades the ten directions in the horizontal dimension.

These preceding six chapters all constitute the merits of the bodhisattva stages, which are the causes for Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*). When these five subsequent [chapters] are accomplished, the principle and the text are both fused, and the fruit of Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*) is fulfilled. As one is about to achieve Sublime Enlightenment, one first realizes the Sublime Dharma; therefore, there is the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Inconceivable Dharma."
Once the Wondrous Dharma is established, one must necessarily achieve the Wondrous Body; hence there is the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies.
Once the Great Marks are perfected, the next stage clarifies the Virtue of the Minor Marks; thus there is the "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Anuvyañjanas."
Once the ferries and bridges are prepared, the merit lies in the act of ferrying others across; when the benefit to all beings is impartial, there is the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra.
When Samantabhadra resides within the mind, the manifestation of the fruit must appear, and thus there is the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata."

The eighth assembly does not depart from the previous location; it is held once again in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsamaṇḍala*). This sutra contains one chapter titled "Leaving the World" (*Lokottara*).

It is said that while the preceding seven assemblies generated understanding through the teaching of differentiated dharmas, this assembly focuses on establishing perfect and harmonious practice based upon that understanding. Therefore, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva poses two hundred questions, to which Samantabhadra Bodhisattva replies with two thousand practices.

Although they cultivate the methods of all practices, these are without intrinsic nature and devoid of marks; yet, while constantly migrating within the world, they are called "those who have transcended the world.

In the ninth stage, the Immovable, at the site of enlightenment of tranquil extinction, they manifest the assembly at Jetavana Grove. There is one chapter in the sutra titled "Entering the Dharma Realm."
This means that whereas previously he had departed from the mundane world, he now enters the Dharma-realm, which is the clear realization.
The Buddha enters the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi because he wishes to cause the great assembly to suddenly realize the Universal Gate.

Therefore, the Great Being Mañjuśrī emerged from the Well-Situated Pavilion and traveled south to convert beings; at the site of an ancient Buddha stupa east of the City of Blessings, he gathered a great multitude of followers.

Regarding those who have resolved their minds on Bodhicitta, there is only the youth Sudhana, who traveled through one hundred and ten cities, encountered spiritual friends, and in each case attained samādhis and gates of liberation.
This culminates in Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, who, at each and every tip of a hair, suddenly realizes liberation, encompassing it all within the ocean of the fruition.
Furthermore, among these nine assemblies, the first assembly presents the Buddha who is the object of faith;
the second assembly presents the mind that is capable of faith.
In the third assembly, understanding arises based on faith;
in the fourth assembly, practice is initiated based on understanding;
and in the fifth assembly, vows are generated based on practice.
In the sixth assembly, the three stages of the worthy ones reach their culmination, and one is about to ascend to the ground of the sages;
in the seventh assembly, causes are subsumed and the fruit is realized;
in the eighth assembly, existence and non-existence are both extinguished, such that they cannot be divided into the categories of reality and delusion.
In the ninth assembly, the realm and wisdom are of one suchness; how could they be reached by the means of a net or a snare?

Furthermore, speaking generally: the first assembly presents the two retributions—the environment and its inhabitants—as the Buddha who is the object of faith, while the ninth assembly clarifies that the one who possesses this faith is the person capable of attaining Buddhahood. Thus, the first and final assemblies together constitute a single meaning, which is precisely the word "Buddha" in the title.
From the second assembly to the eighth assembly, these represent the causes of that Buddha, and thus they are titled using Chinese characters.
Because there are gradations in the causes, seven assemblies are used to illustrate them;
because the fruition has no limits, it is realized by the single Buddha alone.
"Adornment" (yán) means that by means of the causal flowers of vows and practice, one adorns that fruit of Buddhahood which is the Dharma-body.

Furthermore, "Buddha-Flower-Adornment" (Fóhuá-yán) refers to the person who transmits the Dharma; "Great, Square, and Vast" (Dàfāngguǎng) refers to the teaching of the Dharma that is transmitted. When the Dharma constitutes the person, it is called "Great, Square, and Vast" first;
when the person transmits the Dharma, it is called "Buddha-Flower-Adornment."
Among humans, he who gathers the causes and realizes the fruit is none other than the Buddha;
within the Dharma, that which gathers function and returns to the essence is none other than the Great (Mahā).

The "Great" is the Dharmadhātu that is realized, and the "Buddha" is the great wisdom that realizes it. The Buddha and the Great are like light and space: there is no light outside of space, and no Buddha outside of the Great. Space and light are one essence; the Buddha and the Great are in profound accord, indivisible.
It cannot be reached by the mind as an object of perception, nor can it be attained through verbal expression; yet, because it can explain this meaning, it is therefore called a *sūtra*.
This is such that the teaching is established because of the principle, and the principle is perceived because of the teaching.
The Sūtra says: "Just as by the light of the sun, one sees the solar disk;
so by the light of the Buddha’s wisdom, one sees the path traversed by the Buddha.
Because the Buddha is eternal, the Dharma of the Sūtras is also eternal.
The reason for this is that it has never been the case that he abandons his radiance.
As the Sūtra says: "The people of Jambudvīpa see the rising and setting of the sun, though it is separated from them by Mount Sumeru."
"Those who dwell in the midst of the sun always follow the sun and have no rising or setting.
Ordinary beings, separated by ignorance, perceive the Buddha as appearing and disappearing;
the great Bodhisattvas, however, constantly follow the Buddha and experience neither appearance nor disappearance.
The solar orb is the essence, and its radiance is the function; there has never been an essence that does not possess its function.
Because this functional radiance exists, the practitioner perceives the Path and accomplishes what is to be done.
The Buddha-dharma is likewise: its essence is the teaching, and its function is the expounding of that dharma. There has never been a Buddha who did not preach the sutras.
Through hearing and reflecting upon the Dharma, one comes to know the path of liberation; by practicing ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, all are fully accomplished.
The Sūtra says: "Suppose there were a great scripture, equal in size to the three thousandfold world system, contained within a single mote of dust; so it is with every mote of dust.
A wise person, with pure eyes that see all clearly, breaks open the dust and brings forth the scripture, extensively benefiting sentient beings."
Therefore, it is called the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya*.

However, as its textual expressions and meanings are profound and difficult to present in their entirety, I have merely offered this praise based on my own limited experience of seeing and hearing it.
Should even a single phrase or verse herein accord with the ultimate principle, I humbly pray that its blessings may be boundless, providing supreme support for the longevity of the Sage’s life.

On the twenty-first day of the fourth month in the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era, the śramaṇa Jingju of Anguo Temple respectfully presented this work. On the third day of the seventh month in the year of Xinxou, it was transcribed according to the original text transmitted within the ancient repository of Gaoshan Monastery; it was completed after one proofreading on the sixth day.
Written by Daodong of Shanyao Temple at Meicun on the Western Mountain.
